articles.text: MĚIGUÓ RÉN: Nǐmende dàozi pǐnzhǒng hěn duō ma!
AMERICAN: You have so many varieties of rice!
GŌNGZUÒ RÉNYUÁN: Pǐnzhǒng shi bù shǎo, chǎnliàng bǐjiào gāode shi zhèi shíjǐzhǒng.
WORKER: Yes, there are a lot of varieties. The ones with the highest yields are these ten or so here.
MĚIGUÓ RÉN: Tāmende chǎnliàng zài zhèr yǒu méiyou xiězhe?
AMERICAN: Are their yields written down here?
GŌNGZUÒ RÉNYUÁN: Xiězhe ne! Nín xiànzài kàndàode shi Jīngxīdào, mǔchǎn yìqiān yìbǎi jīn zuǒyòu.
WORKER: Yes. What you're looking at now is Capital-West Rice. It has a per-mǔ yield of approximately 1,100 catties.
MĚIGUÓ RÉN: Ou, zhè jiù shi Qiānjīndàode yìzhǒng le.
AMERICAN: Oh, this is one kind of Thousand-Catty Rice.
GŌNGZUÒ RÉNYUÁN: Ng. Jīngxīdàode tèdiǎn jiù shi hǎo chī. "Qiānjīndào" zhèige míngcí zuì zǎo shi zài Jiāngnán yòngde. Xiànzài Jiāngnán dàozi chǎnliàng hái shi bǐjiào gāo yìxiē.

WORKER: Mm. Capital-West Rice is distinguished for being good to eat. The term Thousand-Catty Rice was first used in Jiāngnán (the area south of the lower reaches of the Yangtze River). Today the yield of rice in that area is still comparatively high.
MĚIGUÓ RÉN: Duì, Jiāngnán duōbànr shi píngyuán, méiyou shénme shāndì, shuǐ yòu fāngbian, nóngyè shēngchǎn fāzhǎnqilai bǐjiào yǒu tiáojiàn.
AMERICAN: Of course. Jiāngnán is mostly flatlands. There are hardly any hills. Water is convenient, too. The conditions are better for the development of agriculture.
GŌNGZUÒ RÉNYUÁN: Jiù shi ma! Suǒyǐ Jiāngnán yìzhí shi wǒ guó zhòngyàode nóngyèqū.
WORKER: Exactly! That's why Jiāngnán has always been an important agricultural region of our country.
MĚIGUÓ RÉN: Búguò, wǒ xiǎng xiànzài Huáng Hé liǎng'ànde nóngyè shēngchǎn qíngkuàng yě bú cuò le. Tīngshuō, xiànzài liángshi měimǔ píngjūn chǎnliàng dōu zài sì-wǔbǎijīn zuǒyòu le.
AMERICAN: But I think that now agricultural production is quite good on both sides of the Yellow River. I hear that the average per-mǔ yield of grain is now around four or five hundred catties.
GŌNGZUÒ RÉNYUÁN: Chàbuduō shi zhèiyàng. Wǒ xiǎng zài guò jǐnián qíngkuàng huì gèng hǎo yìxiē.
WORKER: That's about the way it is. And I think that in another few years the situation will be even better.
MĚIGUÓ RÉN: Shíduōnián qián wǒ tīngshuōguo Shǎnxī yíge shēngchǎn dàduì nàr chàbuduō quán shi shāndì, méiyou jǐmǔ dì shi píngde, kěshi tāmen měinián yě mài gěi guójiā bù shǎode liángshi ne!

AMERICAN: Ten or so years ago I heard about a production brigade in Shǎnxī that was almost all on hilly land. There were only a few mǔ of flat land, but they still sold a lot of grain to the state every year!
GŌNGZUÒ RÉNYUÁN: Xiànzài, zhèiyàngde dàduì, gōngshè bù shǎo le. Cháng Jiāng, Jiāngnán, Huáng Hé dìqū nǎr dōu yǒu a!
WORKER: These days, there are a lot of brigades and communes like that. They're everywhere — the Yangtze River, Jiāngnán, and the Yellow River area.
MĚIGUÓ RÉN: Ng, bú cuò bú cuò, Zhōngguóde nóngyè dà yǒu xīwàng!
AMERICAN: Mm, great, great. China's agriculture has a great future!
